reasoning:
Law

 
The application for annulment

27
 In support of her action, the applicant relies on six pleas in law, alleging, first, a manifest error of assessment; second, infringement of the obligation to state reasons; third, infringement of the right to be heard; fourth, breach of the principle of proportionality; fifth, infringement of the fundamental right to freedom of movement laid down in Article 21 TFEU, of Article 52(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (‘the Charter’) and of the constitutional traditions common to the Member States; and, sixth, infringement of the right to property, of Article 52(1) of the Charter, of the constitutional traditions common to the Member States and breach of the right to private life.

 
The second plea, alleging infringement of the obligation to state reasons

28
 By her second plea, the applicant claims, in essence, that the grounds on which the contested acts are based are not sufficiently explained and consequently infringe the second paragraph of Article 296 TFEU.

29
 In that connection, as specifically regards her shareholding in SCI Ruth and in Maples S.A., she states that the evidence in WK maintenance file 2 was not disclosed by the Council, with the result that it was impossible for her to ascertain the precise evidence on which the Council’s conviction was based.

30
 She maintains that the mere reference to the existence of real estate and property ties is not sufficient to characterise in itself the existence of an association. She adds that the Council has failed to demonstrate how she has benefitted, in her capacity as founder and by her participation in the activities of the foundation which she created with her husband (‘the Timchenko Foundation’), from the enhancement of her husband’s public image.

31
 She claims, lastly, that the Council did not especially state the reasons why it considered that her funds must be frozen or the reasons why it was necessary to prohibit her from entering or transiting through the territories of the Member States of the European Union; nor did it provide the reasons why, in its view, such restrictions are such as to put pressure on the Russian authorities.

32
 The Council, supported by the Commission, disputes those arguments.

33
 According to the case-law, the purpose of the obligation to state the reasons on which an act adversely affecting an individual is based, which is a corollary of the principle of respect for the rights of the defence, is, first, to provide the person concerned with sufficient information to make it possible to ascertain whether the act is well founded or whether it is vitiated by a defect which may permit its legality to be contested before the Courts of the European Union and, second, to enable those courts to review the legality of that act (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 63 and the case-law cited).

34
 The statement of reasons required by Article 296 TFEU must be appropriate to the act at issue and the context in which it was adopted. The requirements to be satisfied by the statement of reasons depend on the circumstances of each case, in particular the content of the measure in question, the nature of the reasons given and the interest which the addressees of the measure, or other parties to whom it is of direct and individual concern, may have in obtaining explanations. In particular, it is not necessary for the reasoning to go into all the relevant facts and points of law or to provide a detailed answer to the considerations set out by the person concerned when consulted prior to the adoption of that same measure, since the question whether the statement of reasons is sufficient must be assessed with regard not only to its wording but also to its context and to all the legal rules governing the matter in question. Consequently, the reasons given for a measure adversely affecting a person are sufficient if that measure was adopted in a context which was known to that person and which enables him or her to understand the scope of the measure concerning him or her (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 64 and the case-law cited).

35
 Thus, the degree of precision of the statement of the reasons for a measure must be weighed against practical realities and the time and technical facilities available for taking the measure (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 65 and the case-law cited).

36
 It has been made clear in the case-law that the statement of reasons for an act of the Council which imposes a restrictive measure must identify not only the legal basis for that measure but also the actual and specific reasons why the Council considered, in the exercise of its discretion, that such a measure had to be adopted in respect of the person concerned (see judgment of 27 July 2022, 
RT France
 v 
Council
, T‐125/22, EU:T:2022:483, paragraph 105 and the case-law cited).

37
 In addition, it must be remembered that the obligation to state the reasons on which a measure is based is an essential procedural requirement, which must be distinguished from the question whether the reasons are well founded, which is concerned with the substantive legality of the measure at issue (see, to that effect, judgment of 2 April 1998, 
Commission
 v 
Sytraval and Brink’s France
, C‐367/95 P, EU:C:1998:154, paragraph 67). The reasoning of a decision consists in a formal statement of the grounds on which that decision is based. If those grounds are vitiated by errors, the latter will vitiate the substantive legality of the decision, but not the statement of reasons in it, which may be adequate even though it sets out reasons which are incorrect (see judgment of 18 June 2015, 
Ipatau
 v 
Council
, C‐535/14 P, EU:C:2015:407, paragraph 37 and the case-law cited).

38
 In the present case, it must be stated that both Decision 2014/145 and Regulation No 269/2014 refer to the legal basis on which they are founded, namely Article 29 TEU and Article 215 TFEU, respectively. It should be noted, moreover, that the general context that led the Council to adopt the contested acts is set out in the recitals of those acts.

39
 Furthermore, a reading of the grounds of the contested acts shows those measures were adopted because the Council considered that, through the companies Ruth and Maples and the Timchenko Foundation, and the various real estate acquisitions made with her husband, the applicant was associated with her husband, Mr Timchenko. According to those grounds, the applicant’s husband supports actions and policies that undermine the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine and also provides financial and material support for and benefits from Russian decision-makers who effect such actions and policies. This means that, in the Council’s opinion, the applicant’s husband satisfies criteria (a) and (d).

40
 It follows that the ground of the contested acts allow the applicant to identify not only the legal basis of those acts, but also the actual and specific reasons that led the Council to consider that she is associated with her husband, who himself satisfies the conditions laid down by criteria (a) and (d) and is included on the lists at issue on that basis.

41
 As for the argument that the grounds referred to in paragraph 22 above do not specify the reasons why the Council considered that the applicant’s funds and economic resources must be frozen and her freedom to move within the European Union restricted, it should be observed that it follows from recital 4 of Decision 2014/145 and recitals 3 and 4 of Regulation No 269/2014 that, in view of the worsening of the situation in Ukraine, the European Union decided to adopt such measures in respect, in particular, of persons associated with those undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine, which was sufficient to allow the applicant to understand the reasons why the Council had decided to apply such restrictions to her.

42
 Furthermore, the complaints on which the applicant relies, which consist in claiming, first, that the Council has failed to show how the application of the measures adopted in respect of her would allow the objectives which it pursues in Decision 2014/145 and Regulation No 269/2014 to be attained and, second, that she is unable to ascertain the Council’s understanding as regards the companies Ruth and Maples, are tantamount to calling into question the justification for the measures at issue, which goes to the question whether the measures are well founded and not to the formal statement of reasons for those measures.

43
 It follows from the foregoing that the second plea must be rejected.

 
The third plea, alleging infringement of the right to be heard

44
 By her third plea, the applicant claims that her right to be heard was not respected and, on the contrary, was abused by the Council.

45
 To that end, the applicant claims that the Council did not take into account the arguments which she set out in her letters of 20 January, 15 February and 2 March 2023 in response to the proposals to extend the restrictive measures.

46
 In her reply, the applicant states that the Council has failed to prove that it forwarded her comments and requests for consideration to all the delegations of which it is composed. She claims that if those delegations had been aware of those comments, she would not have been made subject to the contested acts which maintain her name on the lists at issue.

47
 The Council, supported by the Commission, disputes those arguments.

48
 In that regard, it should be observed that the right to be heard in all proceedings, provided for in Article 41(2)(a) of the Charter, which is inherent in respect for the rights of the defence, guarantees every person the opportunity to make known his or her views effectively during an administrative procedure and before the adoption of any decision liable to affect his or her interests adversely (see, to that effect, judgments of 11 December 2014, 
Boudjlida
, C‐249/13, EU:C:2014:2431, paragraphs 34 and 36, and of 18 June 2020, 
Commission
 v 
RQ
, C‐831/18 P, EU:C:2020:481, paragraphs 65 and 67 and the case-law cited).

49
 In proceedings relating to the adoption of the decision to list or maintain the listing of the name of an individual in the annex to an act imposing restrictive measures, respect for the rights of the defence and the right to effective judicial protection requires that the competent EU authority disclose to the individual concerned the evidence against that person available to that authority and relied on as the basis of its decision, so that that individual is in a position to defend his or her rights in the best possible conditions and to decide, with full knowledge of the relevant facts, whether there is any point in bringing an action before the Courts of the European Union. When that disclosure takes place, the competent EU authority must ensure that that individual is placed in a position in which he or she may effectively make known his or her views on the grounds advanced against him or her (judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraphs 111 and 112; see also, to that effect, judgment of 12 December 2006, 
Organisation des Modjahedines du peuple d’Iran
 v 
Council
, T‐228/02, EU:T:2006:384, paragraph 93).

50
 Article 52(1) of the Charter nonetheless allows limitations on the exercise of the rights enshrined in the Charter, subject to the conditions that the limitation concerned respects the essence of the fundamental right in question and, subject to the principle of proportionality, that it is necessary and genuinely meets objectives of general interest recognised by the European Union (see judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 101 and the case-law cited).

51
 Furthermore, the question whether there is a breach of the rights of the defence must be examined in relation to the specific circumstances of each particular case, including the nature of the act at issue, the context of its adoption and the legal rules governing the matter in question (see, to that effect, judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 102 and the case-law cited). The right to be heard prior to the adoption of acts maintaining a person’s or an entity’s name on a list of persons or entities subject to restrictive measures is necessary where, in the decision maintaining that person’s or that entity’s name on that list, the Council has included new evidence against that person or that entity, namely evidence which was not taken into account in the initial decision to include the name on the list (see judgment of 12 February 2020, 
Amisi Kumba
 v 
Council
, T‐163/18, EU:T:2020:57, paragraph 54 and the case-law cited; see also, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 7 April 2016, 
Central Bank of Iran
 v 
Council
, C‐266/15 P, EU:C:2016:208, paragraph 33).

52
 In addition, when comments are made by the individual concerned on the summary of reasons, the competent European Union authority is under an obligation to examine, carefully and impartially, whether the alleged reasons are well founded, in the light of those comments and any exculpatory evidence provided with those comments (judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 114).

53
 In the present case, it should be observed that the evidence in the file is capable of showing that, contrary to the applicant’s contentions, the Council communicated to all its delegations the applicant’s letters of 20 January, 15 February and 2 March 2023.

54
 Furthermore, it follows from the Council’s letters to the applicant, and in particular the letter of 14 March 2023, that contrary to what she argues, the Council examined and replied to the objections raised against the maintenance of the measures.

55
 In addition, it should be observed that the applicant has failed specify how the Council did not respond to her arguments, and it must be borne in mind that the right to be heard does not amount to the right for the applicant’s argument to prevail (see judgment of 14 September 2022, 
SŽ – Tovorni promet
 v 
Commission
, T‐575/20, not published, EU:T:2022:551, paragraph 42 and the case-law cited).

56
 Thus, since none of the evidence on which the applicant relies shows that the Commission infringed her right to be heard, the third plea must be rejected.

 
The first plea, alleging a manifest error of assessment

57
 By her first plea, the applicant claims that, in considering that she is associated with her husband, the Council made a manifest error of assessment, in circumstances in which, according to the case-law, a matrimonial relationship cannot in itself characterise the existence of an association between two spouses.

58
 As regards, in the first place, the applicant’s property ties with her husband, she submits that the Council has failed to prove the allegations which it puts forward, either because the companies in question have ceased all activities or because the members of those companies do not include Mr Timchenko.

59
 As regards, in the second place, the applicant’s role in the Timchenko Foundation, she claims that her role as an administrator on the board of trustees means that she has only a supervisory role in that structure and not, as the Court states in the judgment of 6 September 2023, 
Timchenko
 v 
Council
 (T‐361/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:502), that she is directly linked with the operational activities of that foundation. Furthermore, the creation of a foundation is a normal activity of a wealthy married couple. In the present case, the fact that Mr Timchenko has no active role in the Timchenko Foundation, that foundation does not in any way constitute a tool designed to promote his image or to participate in his public affairs.

60
 In the reply, the applicant maintains her position on that topic.

61
 In that regard, first, she claims that the Timchenko Foundation is required to act in concert the Russian public authorities in order to ensure the efficiency of its activities for vulnerable demographic groups, which it tries to protect. It is in the same desire for efficiency and with the intention of creating synergies that the members of the foundation carry out, 
pro bono
, advisory functions within public bodies of the Russian Federation.

62
 Second, she submits that, even if the Council proved that the Timchenko Foundation conferred a public image on Mr Timchenko, it does not, however, describe how such an image would be capable of serving him in both his personal and professional life.

63
 Third, the applicant claims that, in the judgment of 6 September 2023, 
Timchenko
 v 
Council
 (T‐361/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:502), the General Court gave too broad an interpretation of the concept of ‘association’, whereas, in the judgment of 6 September 2023, 
Pumpyanskaya
 v 
Council
 (T‐272/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:491), it characterised the existence of an association more strictly.

64
 Fourth, as regards the Council’s contention that the importance of the property ties and the family management of the assets are such as to characterise the existence of an association, on the ground that numerous Russian billionaires make use of various legal arrangements in order to circumvent restrictive measures, the applicant claims that the Council’s reasoning is tantamount to creating a presumption of circumvention. She argues that the introduction of such a presumption is not possible, since Decision 2014/145 makes no express provision to that effect.

65
 The Council, supported by the Commission, disputes those arguments.

66
 As a preliminary point, it should be observed that the first plea must be regarded as alleging an error of assessment and not a manifest error of assessment. While it is true that the Council has a degree of discretion to determine on a case-by-case basis whether the legal criteria on which the restrictive measures at issue are based are met, the fact remains that the Courts of the European Union must ensure the review, in principle the full review, of all EU acts (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 121 and the case-law cited).

67
 It must also be recalled that the effectiveness of the judicial review guaranteed by Article 47 of the Charter requires in particular that the Courts of the European Union are to ensure that the decision by which restrictive measures were adopted or maintained, which affects individually the person or entity concerned, is taken on a sufficiently solid factual basis. That entails a verification of the factual allegations in the summary of reasons underpinning that decision, with the consequence that judicial review cannot be restricted to an assessment of the cogency in the abstract of the reasons relied on, but must concern whether those reasons, or, at the very least, one of those reasons, deemed sufficient in itself to support that decision, are substantiated (judgments of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 119, and of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 122).

68
 It is the task of the competent EU authority to establish, in the event of challenge, that the reasons relied on against the person or entity concerned are well founded, and not the task of that person or entity to adduce evidence of the negative, that those reasons are not well founded (judgments of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 121, and of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 123).

69
 In addition, the assessment of whether those reasons are well founded must be carried out by examining the evidence and information not in isolation but in their context. The Council discharges the burden of proof borne by it if it presents to the Courts of the European Union a set of indicia sufficiently specific, precise and consistent to establish that there is a sufficient link between the person subject to a fund-freezing measure and the regime or, in general, the situations, being combated (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 124 and the case-law cited).

70
 Furthermore, restrictive measures are of a precautionary and, by definition, provisional nature, and their validity always depends on whether the factual and legal circumstances which led to their adoption continue to apply and on the need to maintain them in order to achieve their objective. It is thus for the Council, in the course of its periodic review of those restrictive measures, to conduct an updated assessment of the situation and to appraise the impact of such measures, in order to determine whether they have made it possible to attain the objectives pursued by the initial inclusion of the names of the persons and entities concerned on the lists at issue or whether the same conclusion in respect of those persons and entities can still be drawn (see judgment of 26 October 2022, 
Ovsyannikov
 v 
Council
, T‐714/20, not published, EU:T:2022:674, paragraph 67 and the case-law cited).

71
 In order to justify maintaining a person’s name on the lists in question, the Council is not prohibited from basing its decision on the same evidence that justified the initial inclusion, re-inclusion or previous maintenance of the name of the person concerned on those lists, provided that (i) the grounds for inclusion remain unchanged and (ii) the context has not changed in such a way that that evidence is now out of date. That context includes not only the situation of the country in respect of which the system of restrictive measures was established, but also the particular situation of the person concerned. Similarly, maintenance on the list at issue is justified in the light of all the relevant circumstances and, in particular, of the fact that the objectives pursued by the restrictive measures have not been attained (see, to that effect, judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 169 and the case-law cited).

72
 In such a context, the Council may decide to maintain the names of the persons concerned on the lists at issue for the same reasons relating to past acts relied on in previous decisions concerning those persons, provided that the maintenance of their names is still justified in the light of all the relevant circumstances and, in particular, of the fact that the objectives pursued by the restrictive measures have not been attained (see, by analogy, judgment of 8 March 2023, 
Mutondo
 v 
Council
, T‐94/22, not published, EU:T:2023:120, paragraph 50 and the case-law cited).

73
 In the present case, it should be observed, by way of a preliminary point, that by judgment of today, delivered in the case 
Timchenko
 v 
Council
 (T‐297/23), the Court dismissed the action brought by Mr Timchenko against, in particular, Decision 2023/572 and Implementing Regulation 2023/571, pursuant to which his name was included on the lists at issue in respect of criteria (a) and (d).

74
 It should be emphasised, moreover, that although the concept of ‘association’ is often used in acts of the Council relating to restrictive measures, it is not defined as such and its meaning depends on the relevant contexts and circumstances. However, the fact remains that it may be regarded as covering natural or legal persons who are, generally, linked by common interests without any need for a link via an economic activity. The concept of ‘association’ laid down in the relevant provisions of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, and of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/330, may therefore be interpreted as meaning that it covers any natural or legal person or any entity having a link, going beyond a family relationship, with a person subject to restrictive measures on the basis, as in the present case, of providing financial support to or benefiting from Russian decision-makers responsible for the invasion of Ukraine or for supporting actions or policies that undermine or threaten the sovereignty and independence of Ukraine (see judgment of 6 September 2023, 
Timchenko
 v 
Council
, T‐361/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:502, paragraph 74 and the case-law cited).

75
 As regards the applicant specifically, it should be observed that, in order to justify maintaining her name on the lists at issue, the Council relies on the items in the initial WK file, in WK maintenance file 1 and in WK maintenance file 2 and, in particular, on the following items:

– item 2 in the initial WK file: an undated screenshot from the Timchenko Foundation’s page on the website LinkedIn website, to which the Council had access in March 2022;

– item 5 in the initial WK file: a screenshot of a page, undated, on the Timchenko Foundation’s website, accessed by the Council in March 2022;

– item 1 in WK maintenance file 1: a screenshot of an article from the publication 
Business Insider
, dated March 2022, of which the Council became aware in November 2022.

76
 In fact, both item 1 in WK maintenance file 1 and items 2 and 5 in the initial WK file show that Mr and Mrs Timchenko are involved in the Timchenko Foundation. That is confirmed by item 5 in the initial WK file, which proves that, far from being retired from that foundation’s activities, Mr and Mrs Timchenko are personally involved in those activities, since it was they who chose to show themselves publicly to present the association’s activities to visitors to that website.

77
 In addition, the submissions made at the hearing revealed that the applicant was still a member of the board of trustees of the Timchenko Foundation and that, on the date on which the contested acts were adopted, the foundation’s articles of association had not been amended.

78
 That means that, by participating in the board of trustees of the foundation, the applicant is still involved in its administration, irrespective of the fact that her task consists in ‘supervising’ its actions. In addition, as founding members of the Timchenko Foundation, Mr and Mrs Timchenko still have substantial powers within that foundation, in that they may not only obtain information about its activities and have access to its documents, but also appoint and dismiss the members of the foundation’s supervisory board, a body described by the foundation’s charter as the ‘supreme body’.

79
 In addition to those factors, as is apparent from Annex A. 28 to the application, Mr Timchenko, like his wife, is fully associated, in operational terms, with the activity of their eponymous foundation in that, notably during the health crisis linked with the COVID-19 pandemic, he involved the companies of the Volga Group in the foundation’s activities, providing significant financial, logistical and relational support, in this instance, in particular by establishing air links with the People’s Republic of China in order to purchase and distribute various medical materials on behalf of the foundation.

80
 In that regard, it is immaterial that such actions occurred in the specific context of the COVID-19 pandemic. Such intervention is capable of revealing that, in operational terms, Mr Timchenko achieves synergies between the undertakings of his group and the foundation, to supplement the action of the Russian public services. Furthermore, it should be noted that Mr Timchenko, who is one of the leading businesspersons in the Russian Federation, communicates with Russian public opinion concerning such actions, for the greatest benefit of his image.

81
 Such factors are sufficient to establish the existence of an association, within the meaning of the relevant provisions of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Directive 2022/329, and of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/330, within a common legal structure, in particular in that Mr and Mrs Timchenko, as founding members of the Timchenko Foundation, carry out institutional functions within that structure and both put considerable effort into its functioning, especially, in Mr Timchenko’s case, by using the resources of the Volga Group, of which he is the sole shareholder.

82
 In that regard, in the light of the case-law cited in paragraph 74 above, it is irrelevant that the Timchenko Foundation has no commercial aims and that the activity of Mr and Mrs Timchenko in that foundation is voluntary.

83
 Participating in a structure of the size of the Timchenko Foundation, which carries out numerous charitable activities throughout the Russian Federation and which, in order to achieve that aim, has already benefited from the involvement of the undertakings of the Volga Group, constitutes, independently of the extent of the wealth of the spouses concerned, a participation going beyond a mere family link. That analysis is all the more justified because that foundation contributes to giving an enhanced image of Mr and Mrs Timchenko, in particular of Mr Timchenko, in the eyes of Russian public opinion. That means that the Timchenko Foundation may be regarded not only as a benevolent instrument, but also as a communications tool serving the public image of Mr and Mrs Timchenko, which constitutes an enterprise that goes beyond a mere family relationship.

84
 As for recital 7 of Decision 2022/582, it is sufficient to observe that that decision neither adopted nor altered the concept of ‘association’ and that it cannot therefore serve as a basis for the interpretation of that concept.

85
 In addition, as regards the alleged contradiction between the judgments of 6 September 2023, 
Pumpyanskaya
 v 
Council
 (T‐272/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:491), and of 6 September 2023, 
Timchenko
 v 
Council
 (T‐252/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:496), it is sufficient to observe that the circumstances that prevailed in the first of those judgments were different from the circumstances that characterise the situation of Mr and Mrs Timchenko, in that, in the case that gave rise to that judgment, the applicant’s husband had no specific function within the foundation in question, which is not the case here.

86
 In the light of all of those factors, the first plea must be rejected.

 
The fifth plea, concerning infringement of the applicant’s fundamental right to freedom of movement as a Union citizen

87
 By her fifth plea, the applicant claims that the restrictive measures to which she is subject infringe the provisions of Article 21 TFEU, and those of Article 45(1) and Article 52(1) of the Charter.

88
 She submits that, on the basis of Article 29 TEU, it is not possible, in the absence of a special provision to that effect, to restrict the scope of Article 21 TFEU, on the freedom of movement of Union citizens.

89
 In that regard, the applicant claims, in essence, that, contrary to what has already been held in the judgment of 5 November 2014, 
Mayaleh
 v 
Council
 (T‐307/12 and T‐408/13, EU:T:2014:926), restrictive measures adopted on the basis of Article 29 TEU cannot be regarded as a 
lex specialis 
 or as capable of derogating from normative measures adopted on the basis of Article 21 TFEU, including, in particular, Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States amending Regulation (EEC) No 1612/68 and repealing Directives 64/221/EEC, 68/360/EEC, 72/194/EEC, 73/148/EEC, 75/34/EEC, 75/35/EEC, 90/364/EEC, 90/365/EEC and 93/96/EEC (OJ 2004 L 158, p. 77), Article 27 of which allows freedom of movement to be restricted, in compliance with the principle of proportionality, solely on grounds of public policy, public security or public health.

90
 She further claims that analysis of the legislation of various States of the European Union shows that there is a constitutional tradition common to the Member States by virtue of which freedom of movement can be restricted only on grounds of public policy, public security and public health, and subject to strict judicial review.

91
 The applicant infers that the contradiction that exists between the practice of the European Union and that shared constitutional tradition means that the contested acts infringe Article 21 TFEU and Articles 45 and 52 of the Charter.

92
 The Council disputes those arguments.

93
 As a preliminary point, it should be noted that, questioned at the hearing, the applicant stated and confirmed that she was not raising a plea of illegality against Article 1 of Decision 2014/145, in that that article provided that the Member States were to prevent the transit through their territories of persons subject to restrictive measures. She added that she was, however, challenging the legality of the measures to which she was subject in that, in particular, they did not comply with the principle of proportionality.

94
 It should be observed that the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States, enshrined in Article 45(1) of the Charter, is to be exercised, in accordance with Article 52(2) of the Charter, under the conditions and within the limits defined by the Treaties. As is clear from the Explanations relating to the Charter of Fundamental Rights (OJ 2007 C 303, p. 17), the right guaranteed by Article 45(1) of the Charter is the right guaranteed by Article 20(2)(a) TFEU. The scope of that right is explained in Article 21 TFEU.

95
 Under Article 21(1) TFEU, freedom to move and reside within the territory of the Member States is to be exercised subject to the limitations and conditions provided for in the Treaties and by the provisions adopted for their application. As that reservation, formulated in the second part of Article 21(1) TFEU, refers to the Treaties in the plural, it also includes the EU Treaty and the provisions adopted in application of that treaty. It follows that restrictions on the exercise of the right to freedom of movement and of residence of Union citizens enshrined in Article 45(1) of the Charter may be imposed by decisions coming within the common foreign and security policy (CFSP) which are adopted on the basis of Article 29 TFEU, such as Decision 2023/572 (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgments of 5 November 2014, 
Mayaleh
 v 
Council
, T‐307/12 and T‐408/13, EU:T:2014:926, paragraphs 195 and 196, and of 4 December 2015, 
Sarafraz
 v 
Council
, T‐273/13, not published, EU:T:2015:939, paragraphs 194 and 195).

96
 In that regard, it should be observed that, in the field of the CFSP, Article 29 TEU, which is worded in broad terms, authorises the Council to adopt decisions that define the European Union’s position on a particular issue that is geographic or thematic in nature, pursuing the objectives referred to in Article 21(2) TEU, even if that results in a limitation of the freedom of movement of Union citizens within the territory of Member States of which they are not nationals. That means that that freedom may, in application of that article, be restricted on grounds other than those provided for in Directive 2004/38.

97
 That is the position in the present case, since the restrictive measures at issue are intended to exert pressure on the Russian authorities to bring to an end their actions and policies destabilising Ukraine. That is an objective of general interest which falls within those pursued under the CFSP and referred to in Article 21(2)(b) and (c) TEU, such as the consolidation of and support for democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the principles of international law, and the preservation of peace, prevention of conflicts and strengthening of international security and the protection of civilian populations (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 30 November 2016, 
Rotenberg
 v 
Council
, T‐720/14, EU:T:2016:689, paragraph 176).

98
 However, in order to comply with EU law, limitations on the exercise of the rights set forth in Article 45(1) of the Charter must meet the conditions set out in Article 52(1) of the Charter, which means that they must be provided for by law, respect the essence of those rights, pursue an objective of general interest recognised as such by the European Union and not be disproportionate. That consideration also applies to the rights recognised by the Charter for which provision is made in the Treaties (see, to that effect, judgment of 6 October 2015, 
Delvigne
, C‐650/13, EU:C:2015:648, paragraph 46, and Opinion of Advocate General Szpunar in 
Agenzia delle dogane e dei monopoli and Ministero dell’Economia e delle Finanze
, C‐452/20, EU:C:2021:855, point 60). Consequently, limitations on the exercise of the right set forth in Article 45(1) of the Charter, which are imposed in the context of the implementation of the CFSP, must satisfy those conditions.

99
 In the present case, first, the limitations on the applicant’s right to move freely within the territory of the Member States that result from Decision 2023/572 are ‘provided for by law’, since they are set out in an act which is, in particular, of general application, namely Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, and having a clear legal basis in EU law, namely Article 29 TEU.

100
 Second, in so far as concerns the question whether the limitations referred to in paragraph 99 above respect the ‘essence’ of the applicant’s right to move freely within the territory of the Member States, regard must be had to the nature and the scope of the restrictive measures at issue (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 27 July 2022, 
RT France
 v 
Council
, T‐125/22, EU:T:2022:483, paragraph 153).

101
 In that connection, it must be held that the limitations referred to in paragraph 99 above respect the ‘essence’ of the applicant’s right to move freely within the territory of the Member States. First of all, in accordance with Article 1(2) of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, those limitations comply with the principle of international law that a State cannot refuse its own nationals the right to enter its territory and remain there. Next, under Article 6 of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, the lists at issue are to be periodically reviewed so that the names of persons who no longer meet the entry criteria are removed. Last, those limitations do not call into question that right as such, since they have the effect of temporarily suspending, under specific conditions and on account of their individual situations, the right of certain persons to move freely within the territory of the Member States, provided that those conditions continue to be fulfilled (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 6 October 2015, 
Delvigne
, C‐650/13, EU:C:2015:648, paragraph 48).

102
 Third, the limitations referred to in paragraph 99 above are intended to exert pressure on the Russian authorities to bring to an end their actions and policies destabilising Ukraine. That is an objective of general interest which falls within those pursued under the CFSP and referred to in Article 21(2)(b) TEU, such as the consolidation of and support for democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the principles of international law, and the preservation of peace, prevention of conflicts and strengthening of international security and the protection of civilian populations (see, by analogy, judgment of 30 November 2016, 
Rotenberg
 v 
Council
, T‐720/14, EU:T:2016:689, paragraph 176).

103
 Fourth, with regard to the principle of proportionality, it should be recalled that, as a general principle of EU law, this requires that measures adopted by the EU institutions do not exceed the limits of what is appropriate and necessary in order to attain the objectives pursued by the legislation in question. Consequently, where there is a choice between several appropriate measures, recourse must be had to the least onerous, and the disadvantages caused must not be disproportionate to the aims pursued (see judgment of 30 November 2016, 
Rotenberg
 v 
Council
, T‐720/14, EU:T:2016:689, paragraph 178 and the case-law cited).

104
 As regards the necessity of the limitations referred to in paragraph 99 above, it should be noted that the applicant has failed to show that the Council could envisage adopting measures which were less restrictive but just as appropriate as those provided for. Furthermore, the application of the restrictive measures at issue is subject to the exemption mechanism referred to in Article 1(6) of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, which authorises Member States to grant exemptions from the measures imposed, in particular where travel is justified on the ground of urgent humanitarian need.

105
 Moreover, while recognising the negative consequences for the applicant, as described by her, which result from the application of the restrictive measures at issue, it must be held that, in the light of the importance of the objectives pursued by those measures, the limitations referred to in paragraph 99 above are not manifestly disproportionate (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 14 October 2009, 
Bank Melli Iran
 v 
Council
, T‐390/08, EU:T:2009:401, paragraph 71).

106
 In that regard, it must be emphasised that the fact that the applicant cannot enjoy the real estate which she owns in the European Union owing to the restriction of her freedom of movement does not constitute a disproportionate restriction given the importance of the objectives pursued by those measures (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 14 October 2009, 
Bank Melli Iran
 v 
Council
, T‐390/08, EU:T:2009:401, paragraph 71).

107
 Furthermore, it should be observed that, contrary to what the applicant claims, the constitutional traditions common to the Member States do not establish a right for Union citizens to the Union to move within the territory of a State other than that of which they are a national. It follows that the applicant is not justified in maintaining that those traditions are such as to limit the Council’s competence to adopt, in the context of the CFSP, restrictions on the freedom of movement of citizens on grounds other than public policy, public security and public health.

108
 It follows that the limitations on the applicant’s right to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States satisfy the conditions laid down in the Treaties.

109
 In the light of the foregoing, the fifth plea must be rejected.

 
The sixth plea, concerning infringement of Articles 7 and 17 of the Charter in the light of the right to property and the right to respect for private life and the constitutional traditions common to the Member States

110
 By her sixth plea, the applicant claims that the restrictive measures to which she is subject infringe Articles 7 and 17 of the Charter, which protect the right to respect for private life and the right to property.

111
 She submits that the infringement of the right to property was aggravated by the fact that, by Regulation (EU) 2022/1273 of 21 July 2022 amending Regulation No 269/2014 (OJ 2022 L 194, p. 1), the Council inserted in Regulation No 269/2014 a new Article 9, paragraphs 2 and 3 of which require persons whose names are on the lists at issue to report funds or economic resources within the jurisdiction of a Member State that belong to or are owned, held or controlled by them; any failure to report such funds or resources is to be regarded as a circumvention of the restrictive measures.

112
 She states that the application of the provisions of Article 9(2) of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/1273, along with those of Article 15(1) of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Council Regulation (EU) 2022/880 of 3 June 2022 (OJ 2022 L 153, p. 75), is liable to create a risk that her assets and possessions will be confiscated.

113
 She claims that the infringement of the right to property by the restrictive measures constitutes an unlawful interference in the light of the constitutional traditions common to the Member States.

114
 To that end, she states that national laws authorise the freezing of assets and possessions only on condition that there is a causal link between the personal conduct of the individual and the frozen property or asset, which may be the case, for example, where an asset has enabled an offence to be carried out or is the result of that offence.

115
 She claims, furthermore, that the restrictive measures to which she is subject damage her reputation and therefore entail an infringement of the right to respect for her private life. To that end, she claims that she was associated with the actions of her husband and linked, in the eyes of public opinion, with the actions which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence in Ukraine, although she is not connected with the situations combated by the European Union.

116
 As a preliminary point, it should be noted that the applicant does not raise a plea of illegality against the provisions of Regulation No 269/2014 and those of Decision 2014/145, which provide for the freezing of the property and assets of the persons whose names are included on the lists at issue and for the exemptions from those fund-freezing measures, nor does she dispute, by means of a plea, the legality of Article 9(2) of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/1273, with Article 15(1) of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/880.

117
 Thus, as the applicant has failed to raise, by means of a plea, the illegality of those provisions, the Court cannot invalidate the restrictive measures to which she is subject on the grounds that the provisions on which those measures are based are illegal.

118
 As regards, moreover, the infringement of the right to private life and the right to property by the restrictive measures at issue, it should be observed that those measures are precautionary measures which are not intended to deprive the persons concerned of those rights, enshrined in Article 7 and Article 17 of the Charter, respectively. However, those measures undeniably entail a restriction of those fundamental rights in the present case (see, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 12 March 2014, 
Al Assad
 v 
Council
, T‐202/12, EU:T:2014:113, paragraph 115 and the case-law cited).

119
 Nonetheless, as stated in paragraph 98 above, in order to comply with EU law, limitations on the exercise of the rights enshrined in the Charter must meet the conditions laid down in Article 52(1) thereof, namely that those measures must be provided for by law, respect the essence of those rights, pursue an objective of general interest recognised as such by the European Union, and not be disproportionate.

120
 In the present case, it is clear that those four conditions are satisfied.

121
 First, it must be noted that the limitations on the applicant’s exercise of her right to property and the breach of her right to respect for her private life are ‘provided for by law’, since they are set out in acts that are, inter alia, of general application, namely Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, and Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/330, and which have a clear legal basis in EU law, namely Article 29 TEU and Article 215 TFEU, respectively.

122
 Second, since the contested acts apply for six months and are kept under constant review, as provided for in Article 6 of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, the limitations referred to in paragraph 121 above are temporary and reversible. It must therefore be held that they do not infringe the essence of her right to respect for private and family life or her right to property. In addition, the contested acts provide for the possibility of granting exemptions from the restrictive measures applied. In particular, with regard to the freezing of funds, Article 2(3) and (4) of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, and Article 4(1), Article 5(1) and Article 6(1) of Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/330, provide for the possibility, first, of authorising the use of frozen funds to meet essential needs or to satisfy certain commitments and, second, of granting specific authorisations to unfreeze funds, other financial assets or other economic resources.

123
 Third, the limitations referred to in paragraph 121 are intended to attain the objective of general interest referred to in paragraph 102 above.

124
 Fourth, as regards the appropriateness of those limitations, first of all, it should be observed that they are appropriate for attaining the objective of general interest referred to in paragraph 102 above, in that they contribute to its attainment. Next, as regards their necessity, it should be noted that the applicant does not mention any alternative and less restrictive measures that would be as effective in achieving the objectives pursued. Lastly, the restrictions in question are temporary and reversible and provide for possible exemptions. Accordingly, it must be held that the disadvantages caused to the applicant are not disproportionate in view of the importance of the objective pursued by those acts.

125
 Furthermore, the argument put forward by the applicant on the basis that there are constitutional traditions common to the Member States with respect to the right to property must be rejected. Aside from the fact that the applicant relies on a limited number of analyses of the national laws of the Member States, it should be observed that she has failed to show that those national laws require compliance with conditions that are essentially different from those laid down in Article 52(1) of the Charter.

126
 Having regard to the foregoing, the sixth plea must be rejected in its entirety.

 
The fourth plea, concerning breach of the principle of proportionality

127
 By her fourth plea, the applicant claims, in essence, that the measures at issue breach the principle of proportionality in that they are neither appropriate nor necessary. She further claims that the interpretation of the concept of ‘association’ given by the Council is too broad, in so far as she is not involved in actions or policies undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine and she has no power to influence the policies that lead to such actions.

128
 In that connection, first of all, it should be observed that, for the reasons already stated in paragraphs 104, 105 and 124 above, the restrictive measures at issue are necessary and appropriate and do not constitute a breach of the principle of proportionality.

129
 Next, as regards the complaints that the concept of ‘association’ is interpreted too broadly and that the applicant exercises no influence over Russian decision-makers, it must be observed that since the Council considered, without making an error of assessment, that the applicant was associated with her husband through the Timchenko Foundation, it was entitled to impose on her the restrictive measures to which she is subject.

130
 Lastly, in so far as concerns the restrictive measures taken against her, irrespective of the fact that the applicant denies being at the root of the actions or policies pursued by the leaders of the Russian Federation or being able to exercise any influence whatsoever over them, it should be observed that the restrictions on freedom to move within the Member States of the European Union, like the freezing of the funds or resources of the persons whose names are included on the lists at issue, are such as to exert pressure not only on those persons, but also on the general functioning of the Russian economy and, ultimately, at least indirect pressure on the leaders of the Russian Federation.

131
 It follows that the fourth plea, and the claim for annulment in its entirety, must be rejected.

 
The claim for compensation

132
 In support of this claim, the applicant submits that the contested acts caused her to suffer non-material damage in respect of which she seeks compensation.

133
 The Council contends that this claim must be rejected.

134
 It should be borne in mind that, according to settled case-law, in order for the European Union to incur non-contractual liability for the unlawful conduct of its organs, within the meaning of the second paragraph of Article 340 TFEU, a number of conditions must be satisfied: the institutions’ conduct must be unlawful, actual damage must have been suffered and there must be a causal link between the conduct and the damage pleaded. Since those three conditions for the incurring of liability are cumulative, failure to meet one of them is sufficient for an action for damages to be dismissed, without there being any need to examine the other conditions (see judgment of 22 June 2022, 
Haswani
 v 
Council
, T‐479/21, not published, EU:T:2022:383, paragraph 155 and the case-law cited).

135
 As regards the damage which the applicant claims to have suffered as a result of the adoption of the contested acts, it follows from the findings set out above in relation to the claim for annulment that the maintenance of the applicant’s name on the lists at issue is not vitiated by illegality. Accordingly, since one of the conditions referred to in paragraph 134 above has not been met, the claim for compensation must be rejected.

136
 Having regard to all of the foregoing, that claim must be rejected and the action dismissed in its entirety.

JUDGMENT OF THE GENERAL COURT (First Chamber, Extended Composition)

2 April 2025 (

)

( Common foreign and security policy – Restrictive measures in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine – Freezing of funds – List of persons, entities and bodies subject to the freezing of funds and economic resources – Restrictions on entering the territories of the Member States – List of persons, entities and bodies subject to restrictions on entering the territories of the Member States – Maintenance of the applicant’s name on the lists – Obligation to state reasons – Article 2(1)(a) and (d) of Decision 2014/145/CFSP – Article 3(1)(a) and (d) of Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 – Error of assessment – Right to be heard – Citizenship of the Union – Freedom of movement – Right to property – Proportionality )

In Case T‐298/23,

Elena Petrovna Timchenko,
 residing in Moscow (Russia), represented by T. Bontinck, S. Bonifassi, E. Federova, J. Goffin and J. Bastien, lawyers,

applicant,

v

Council of the European Union,
 represented by M.‐C. Cadilhac and V. Piessevaux, acting as Agents,

defendant,

supported by

European Commission,
 represented by C. Giolito and M. Carpus Carcea, acting as Agents,

intervener,

THE GENERAL COURT (First Chamber, Extended Composition),

composed of R. Mastroianni, acting as President, M. Brkan, I. Gâlea, T. Tóth (Rapporteur) and S.L. Kalėda, Judges,

Registrar: H. Eriksson, Administrator,

having regard to the written procedure,

further to the hearing on 11 June 2024,

gives the following

Judgment

1
 By her action, the applicant, Ms Elena Timchenko, seeks, (i) under Article 263 TFEU, the annulment of Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/572 of 13 March 2023 amending Decision 2014/145/CFSP concerning restrictive measures in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine (OJ 2023 L 75 I, p. 134), and of Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/571 of 13 March 2023 implementing Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 concerning restrictive measures in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine (OJ 2023 L 75 I, p. 1) (together, ‘the contested acts’) and (ii), under Article 268 TFEU, compensation in respect of the non-material harm that the applicant claims to have suffered as a result of the adoption of those acts.

 
Background to the dispute

2
 The applicant is the wife of the businessperson Mr Gennady Nikolayevich Timchenko. They both hold Russian and Finnish nationalities.

3
 The present case arises in the context of restrictive measures adopted by the European Union in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.

4
 On 17 March 2014, the Council of the European Union adopted, on the basis of Article 29 TEU, Decision 2014/145/CFSP concerning restrictive measures in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine (OJ 2014 L 78, p. 16).

5
 On the same day, the Council adopted, on the basis of Article 215 TFEU, Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 concerning restrictive measures in respect of actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine (OJ 2014 L 78, p. 6).

6
 Following the aggression against Ukraine by the armed forces of the Russian Federation, the Council adopted, on 25 February 2022, Decision (CFSP) 2022/329 amending Decision 2014/145 (OJ 2022 L 50, p. 1), in order, inter alia, to adapt the criteria by which natural or legal persons, entities or bodies could be made subject to the restrictive measures at issue.

7
 Article 2(1) and (2) of Decision 2014/145 in the version amended by Decision 2022/329 provides as follows:

‘1. All funds and economic resources belonging to, or owned, held or controlled by:

(a) natural persons responsible for, supporting or implementing actions or policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine, or stability or security in Ukraine, or which obstruct the work of international organisations in Ukraine;

...

(d) natural or legal persons, entities or bodies supporting, materially or financially, or benefiting from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea or the destabilisation of Ukraine;

...

and natural or legal persons, entities or bodies associated with them, as listed in the Annex, shall be frozen.

2. No funds or economic resources shall be made available, directly or indirectly, to or for the benefit of natural or legal persons, entities or bodies listed in the Annex.’

8
 The detailed rules for the freezing of those funds are laid down in the subsequent paragraphs of that article.

9
 Article 1(1)(a) and (b) of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, prohibits the entry into, or transit through, the territories of the Member States of natural persons who satisfy essentially the same criteria as those set out in Article 2(1)(a) and (d) of that decision.

10
 Regulation No 269/2014, in the version amended by Council Regulation (EU) 2022/330 of 25 February 2022 (OJ 2022 L 51, p. 1), requires the adoption of measures for the freezing of funds and sets out the detailed rules for such freezing in terms essentially identical to those of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329. In particular, Article 3(1)(a) and (d) essentially reproduces the same criteria as those set out in Article 2(1)(a) and (d) of Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329 (‘criterion (a)’ and ‘criterion (d)’, respectively).

 
Initial 
inclusion 
and maintenance of the applicant’s name on the lists of restrictive measures until 
13 March
 2023

11
 On 8 April 2022, in view of the gravity of the situation in Ukraine, the Council adopted Decision (CFSP) 2022/582 amending Decision 2014/145 (OJ 2022 L 110, p. 55), and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/581 implementing Regulation No 269/2014 (OJ 2022 L 110, p. 3).

12
 Recital 7 of Decision 2022/582 stated the following:

‘In view of the gravity of the situation, the Council considers that it is appropriate to impose restrictive measures on leading businesspersons involved in economic sectors providing a substantial source of revenue to, and on persons supporting or benefiting from, the Government of the Russian Federation and on natural persons associated with those persons, including family members unduly benefiting from them.’

13
 By those acts, and on the basis of WK file 5055/22 (‘the initial WK file’), the applicant’s name was added, under number 903, to the list annexed to Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/329, and, under the same number, to the list in Annex I to Regulation No 269/2014, as amended by Regulation 2022/330 (‘the lists at issue’), on the following grounds:

‘[Ms] Elena [Petrovna] Timchenko is the wife of the billionaire [Mr] Gennady Timchenko, listed under Decision 2014/145 ... She participates in his public affairs via the Timchenko Foundation. She is thus benefiting from [Mr] Gennady Timchenko who is responsible for supporting actions and policies which undermine the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine and for providing financial and material support, and benefitting from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine.’

14
 On 11 April 2022, a notice for the attention of the persons, entities and bodies subject to the restrictive measures provided for by Decision 2014/145, as amended by Decision 2022/582, and Regulation No 269/2014, as implemented by Implementing Regulation 2022/581, was published in the 
Official Journal of the European Union 
(OJ 2022 C 157, p. 11).

15
 On 14 September 2022, by Decision (CFSP) 2022/1530 amending Decision 2014/145 (OJ 2022 L 239, p. 149), and by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1529 implementing Regulation No 269/2014 (OJ 2022 L 239, p. 1), the Council maintained the restrictive measures to which the applicant was subject.

16
 The applicant brought an action, registered as Case T‐361/22, against Decisions 2022/582 and 2022/1530 and Implementing Regulations 2022/581 and 2022/1529, which was dismissed by judgment of 6 September 2023, 
Timchenko
 v 
Council
 (T‐361/22, not published, under appeal, EU:T:2023:502).

17
 On 22 December 2022, the Council informed the applicant that it intended to maintain her name on the lists at issue. It also sent her file WK 17719/2022 INIT (‘WK maintenance file 1’).

18
 In reply, on 20 January 2023, the applicant sent a letter to the Council, in which she set out her comments on the Council’s intention to maintain her name on the lists at issue.

19
 By letter of 6 February 2023, the Council informed the applicant of its decision to maintain her name on the lists at issue and sent the draft statement of reasons for those maintenance measures along with the file of evidence on which it relied, namely file WK 1326/2023 INIT (‘WK maintenance file 2’).

20
 Following that letter, the applicant submitted her comments to the Council on 15 February 2023. On the same day, the Council replied, confirming that it intended to maintain the measures to which she was subject, on the basis of a statement of reasons which differed from the previous statements.

21
 On 2 March 2023, the applicant submitted her comments to the Council.

 
The adoption of the contested acts

22
 On 13 March 2023, the Council adopted the contested acts, maintaining the applicant’s name, under number 903, on the lists at issue on the following grounds:

‘[Ms] Elena [Petrovna] Timchenko is the wife of [Mr] Gennady [Nikolayevich] Timchenko, a long-time acquaintance of President Vladimir Putin and one of his confidants.

She carries out business activities, together with her husband, through the real estate company SCI Ruth and the company Maples S.A., and acquired real estate jointly with her husband, which demonstrates important property ties between them.

Furthermore, she participates in her husband’s public affairs through the Timchenko Foundation which she co-founded with her husband and in which she plays an important role and she is closely associated with her husband. In addition, this foundation carries out some of its activities in connection with the Volga Group investment group which contributes significantly to the economy [of] Russia and its development and was founded by [Mr] Gennady [Nikolayevich] Timchenko, who is one of its shareholders. [Ms] Elena [Petrovna] Timchenko therefore benefits from her husband, particularly in terms of social position and in financial terms. She is therefore associated with [Mr] Gennady [Nikolayevich] Timchenko, listed under Decision 2014/145 ... on the grounds, inter alia, that he is responsible for supporting actions and policies which undermine the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine and for providing financial and material support, and benefitting from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine.’

23
 On 14 March 2023, the Council informed the applicant that it had adopted the contested acts and replied to her letters of 31 October 2022, 20 January, 15 February and 2 March 2023.

24
 On 23 March 2023, the applicant informed the Council that, unlike the other language versions, the French version of the reasoning set out in paragraph 22 above suggested that she benefitted from Russian decision-makers, which was not the case.

 
Procedure and forms of order sought

25
 The applicant claims that the Court should:

– annul the contested acts;

– order the Council to pay EUR 1 000 000 in compensation for the non-material harm that the applicant has suffered;

– order the Council to pay the costs.

26
 The Council, supported by the European Commission, contends that the Court should:

– dismiss the action in its entirety;

– order the applicant to pay the costs.

Law

 
The application for annulment

27
 In support of her action, the applicant relies on six pleas in law, alleging, first, a manifest error of assessment; second, infringement of the obligation to state reasons; third, infringement of the right to be heard; fourth, breach of the principle of proportionality; fifth, infringement of the fundamental right to freedom of movement laid down in Article 21 TFEU, of Article 52(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (‘the Charter’) and of the constitutional traditions common to the Member States; and, sixth, infringement of the right to property, of Article 52(1) of the Charter, of the constitutional traditions common to the Member States and breach of the right to private life.

 
The second plea, alleging infringement of the obligation to state reasons

28
 By her second plea, the applicant claims, in essence, that the grounds on which the contested acts are based are not sufficiently explained and consequently infringe the second paragraph of Article 296 TFEU.

29
 In that connection, as specifically regards her shareholding in SCI Ruth and in Maples S.A., she states that the evidence in WK maintenance file 2 was not disclosed by the Council, with the result that it was impossible for her to ascertain the precise evidence on which the Council’s conviction was based.

30
 She maintains that the mere reference to the existence of real estate and property ties is not sufficient to characterise in itself the existence of an association. She adds that the Council has failed to demonstrate how she has benefitted, in her capacity as founder and by her participation in the activities of the foundation which she created with her husband (‘the Timchenko Foundation’), from the enhancement of her husband’s public image.

31
 She claims, lastly, that the Council did not especially state the reasons why it considered that her funds must be frozen or the reasons why it was necessary to prohibit her from entering or transiting through the territories of the Member States of the European Union; nor did it provide the reasons why, in its view, such restrictions are such as to put pressure on the Russian authorities.

32
 The Council, supported by the Commission, disputes those arguments.

33
 According to the case-law, the purpose of the obligation to state the reasons on which an act adversely affecting an individual is based, which is a corollary of the principle of respect for the rights of the defence, is, first, to provide the person concerned with sufficient information to make it possible to ascertain whether the act is well founded or whether it is vitiated by a defect which may permit its legality to be contested before the Courts of the European Union and, second, to enable those courts to review the legality of that act (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 63 and the case-law cited).

34
 The statement of reasons required by Article 296 TFEU must be appropriate to the act at issue and the context in which it was adopted. The requirements to be satisfied by the statement of reasons depend on the circumstances of each case, in particular the content of the measure in question, the nature of the reasons given and the interest which the addressees of the measure, or other parties to whom it is of direct and individual concern, may have in obtaining explanations. In particular, it is not necessary for the reasoning to go into all the relevant facts and points of law or to provide a detailed answer to the considerations set out by the person concerned when consulted prior to the adoption of that same measure, since the question whether the statement of reasons is sufficient must be assessed with regard not only to its wording but also to its context and to all the legal rules governing the matter in question. Consequently, the reasons given for a measure adversely affecting a person are sufficient if that measure was adopted in a context which was known to that person and which enables him or her to understand the scope of the measure concerning him or her (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 64 and the case-law cited).

35
 Thus, the degree of precision of the statement of the reasons for a measure must be weighed against practical realities and the time and technical facilities available for taking the measure (see judgment of 15 November 2023, 
OT
 v 
Council
, T‐193/22, EU:T:2023:716, paragraph 65 and the case-law cited).

36
 It has been made clear in the case-law that the statement of reasons for an act of the Council which imposes a restrictive measure must identify not only the legal basis for that measure but also the actual and specific reasons why the Council considered, in the exercise of its discretion, that such a measure had to be adopted in respect of the person concerned (see judgment of 27 July 2022, 
RT France
 v 
Council
, T‐125/22, EU:T:2022:483, paragraph 105 and the case-law cited).

37
 In addition, it must be remembered that the obligation to state the reasons on which a measure is based is an essential procedural requirement, which must be distinguished from the question whether the reasons are well founded, which is concerned with the substantive legality of the measure at issue (see, to that effect, judgment of 2 April 1998, 
Commission
 v 
Sytraval and Brink’s France
, C‐367/95 P, EU:C:1998:154, paragraph 67). The reasoning of a decision consists in a formal statement of the grounds on which that decision is based. If those grounds are vitiated by errors, the latter will vitiate the substantive legality of the decision, but not the statement of reasons in it, which may be adequate even though it sets out reasons which are incorrect (see judgment of 18 June 2015, 
Ipatau
 v 
Council
, C‐535/14 P, EU:C:2015:407, paragraph 37 and the case-law cited).

38
 In the present case, it must be stated that both Decision 2014/145 and Regulation No 269/2014 refer to the legal basis on which they are founded, namely Article 29 TEU and Article 215 TFEU, respectively. It should be noted, moreover, that the general context that led the Council to adopt the contested acts is set out in the recitals of those acts.

39
 Furthermore, a reading of the grounds of the contested acts shows those measures were adopted because the Council considered that, through the companies Ruth and Maples and the Timchenko Foundation, and the various real estate acquisitions made with her husband, the applicant was associated with her husband, Mr Timchenko. According to those grounds, the applicant’s husband supports actions and policies that undermine the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine and also provides financial and material support for and benefits from Russian decision-makers who effect such actions and policies. This means that, in the Council’s opinion, the applicant’s husband satisfies criteria (a) and (d).

40
 It follows that the ground of the contested acts allow the applicant to identify not only the legal basis of those acts, but also the actual and specific reasons that led the Council to consider that she is associated with her husband, who himself satisfies the conditions laid down by criteria (a) and (d) and is included on the lists at issue on that basis.

41
 As for the argument that the grounds referred to in paragraph 22 above do not specify the reasons why the Council considered that the applicant’s funds and economic resources must be frozen and her freedom to move within the European Union restricted, it should be observed that it follows from recital 4 of Decision 2014/145 and recitals 3 and 4 of Regulation No 269/2014 that, in view of the worsening of the situation in Ukraine, the European Union decided to adopt such measures in respect, in particular, of persons associated with those undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine, which was sufficient to allow the applicant to understand the reasons why the Council had decided to apply such restrictions to her.

42
 Furthermore, the complaints on which the applicant relies, which consist in claiming, first, that the Council has failed to show how the application of the measures adopted in respect of her would allow the objectives which it pursues in Decision 2014/145 and Regulation No 269/2014 to be attained and, second, that she is unable to ascertain the Council’s understanding as regards the companies Ruth and Maples, are tantamount to calling into question the justification for the measures at issue, which goes to the question whether the measures are well founded and not to the formal statement of reasons for those measures.

43
 It follows from the foregoing that the second plea must be rejected.

 
The third plea, alleging infringement of the right to be heard

44
 By her third plea, the applicant claims that her right to be heard was not respected and, on the contrary, was abused by the Council.

45
 To that end, the applicant claims that the Council did not take into account the arguments which she set out in her letters of 20 January, 15 February and 2 March 2023 in response to the proposals to extend the restrictive measures.

46
 In her reply, the applicant states that the Council has failed to prove that it forwarded her comments and requests for consideration to all the delegations of which it is composed. She claims that if those delegations had been aware of those comments, she would not have been made subject to the contested acts which maintain her name on the lists at issue.

47
 The Council, supported by the Commission, disputes those arguments.

48
 In that regard, it should be observed that the right to be heard in all proceedings, provided for in Article 41(2)(a) of the Charter, which is inherent in respect for the rights of the defence, guarantees every person the opportunity to make known his or her views effectively during an administrative procedure and before the adoption of any decision liable to affect his or her interests adversely (see, to that effect, judgments of 11 December 2014, 
Boudjlida
, C‐249/13, EU:C:2014:2431, paragraphs 34 and 36, and of 18 June 2020, 
Commission
 v 
RQ
, C‐831/18 P, EU:C:2020:481, paragraphs 65 and 67 and the case-law cited).

49
 In proceedings relating to the adoption of the decision to list or maintain the listing of the name of an individual in the annex to an act imposing restrictive measures, respect for the rights of the defence and the right to effective judicial protection requires that the competent EU authority disclose to the individual concerned the evidence against that person available to that authority and relied on as the basis of its decision, so that that individual is in a position to defend his or her rights in the best possible conditions and to decide, with full knowledge of the relevant facts, whether there is any point in bringing an action before the Courts of the European Union. When that disclosure takes place, the competent EU authority must ensure that that individual is placed in a position in which he or she may effectively make known his or her views on the grounds advanced against him or her (judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraphs 111 and 112; see also, to that effect, judgment of 12 December 2006, 
Organisation des Modjahedines du peuple d’Iran
 v 
Council
, T‐228/02, EU:T:2006:384, paragraph 93).

50
 Article 52(1) of the Charter nonetheless allows limitations on the exercise of the rights enshrined in the Charter, subject to the conditions that the limitation concerned respects the essence of the fundamental right in question and, subject to the principle of proportionality, that it is necessary and genuinely meets objectives of general interest recognised by the European Union (see judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 101 and the case-law cited).

51
 Furthermore, the question whether there is a breach of the rights of the defence must be examined in relation to the specific circumstances of each particular case, including the nature of the act at issue, the context of its adoption and the legal rules governing the matter in question (see, to that effect, judgment of 18 July 2013, 
Commission and Others
 v 
Kadi
, C‐584/10 P, C‐593/10 P and C‐595/10 P, EU:C:2013:518, paragraph 102 and the case-law cited). The right to be heard prior to the adoption of acts maintaining a person’s or an entity’s name on a list of persons or entities subject to restrictive measures is necessary where, in the decision maintaining that person’s or that entity’s name on that list, the Council has included new evidence against that person or that entity, namely evidence which was not taken into account in the initial decision to include the name on the list (see judgment of 12 February 2020, 
Amisi Kumba
 v 
Council
, T‐163/18, EU:T:2020:57, paragraph 54 and the case-law cited; see also, to that effect and by analogy, judgment of 7 April 2016, 
Central Bank of Iran
 v 
Council
, C‐266/15 P, EU:C:2016:208, paragraph 33).

52
